title: Company X-Ray: a company's own documents, read together
one_line: A company drops its own documents into an encrypted vault. Agents run a catalogue of analyses across them, a person reviews the result, and within five working days the company gets back its questions answered, a one-page board pack, findings that each name the document and row they came from, and a Claude setup to keep asking. No connectors, no integrations, no access to anything.

problem.name: The documents exist. Nobody reads them together.
problem.text: Management accounts, a customer list, a complaints log, board minutes, the plan, the supplier list: each has an owner, and nobody sets one against another.

problem.name: The owner has a feeling, not a picture
problem.text: "Busier than ever and making less money." The reason is usually in the documents, a few rows apart in files that never meet.

problem.name: A chat window is not enough
problem.text: Anyone can paste a spreadsheet into an assistant. What they do not get is the right questions, arithmetic that re-runs, every claim tied to its evidence, and a person who checked it.

problem.name: Consultants are slow and dear
problem.text: A reading of the business by an adviser takes weeks and costs thousands. Most small companies never commission one.

problem.name: Integrations stall the sale
problem.text: Connecting to a company's accounts, mail and drive means security reviews and access contracts. Dropping files into a vault means the customer decides what is seen, and the sale closes the same day.

formula.name: An agent platform
formula.text: Claude or ChatGPT, with the operator's catalogue of analyses and prompts.

formula.name: A vault
formula.text: Encrypted on the device, one per customer: the documents in, the X-ray out, and the history of both.

formula.name: Your documents
formula.text: What you choose to send, and nothing more. No connectors, no logins.

formula.name: An X-ray, and a Claude setup
formula.text: Your questions answered, a board pack, evidence for every finding, and a project to keep asking in.

steps.name: Buy, and receive a key
steps.text: A standing payment link per level. The vault key arrives separately from the instructions, never on a page.

steps.name: Drop documents in
steps.text: Into the vault's inbox, with an intake form: why now, three questions, what was sent and what was left out.

steps.name: Agents run the catalogue
steps.text: Twelve analyses. Arithmetic written as a script first, then findings, each labelled and tied to its evidence.

steps.name: A person reviews
steps.text: Runs the script until every figure matches, reads every inferred finding against its evidence, and commits a review note.

steps.name: Delivered to the vault
steps.text: Board pack, X-ray, questions, ninety days. Done is a commit in the customer's history.

steps.name: Keep asking
steps.text: Project instructions and files for a Claude Project, or a ChatGPT Project. The conversation continues with the same evidence and the same rules.

catalogue: Is the business making more or less per month, and since when?
Which line makes the money, and which moved?
When did prices last move, and what moved since?
How much rests on the largest customers?
Which contracts reach a notice or renewal date soon?
Is service getting better or worse, where, and for whom?
Where do the plan, the minutes and the numbers disagree?
Which decisions are recorded and not closed?
Which jobs rest on one person?
What is paid for, duplicated, unowned or unused?
Where is AI used, on what information, under what rule?
What would a board expect to see that was not sent?

phases.text: The invented company X-rayed, published with a read key. The intake page and four payment links.

phases.text: Companies the founder knows. Every hour measured. The catalogue rewritten from what was found and missed.

open_questions: Is £500 right for the Standard level, or does the board pack justify £750?
How many documents does a typical small company have, and in what state?
